claims.text: Under high-temperature plasma-facing conditions, equimolar WTaTiVZr exhibits greater plastic strain than commercially pure tungsten.
Under high-temperature plasma-facing conditions, equimolar WTaTiVZr exhibits greater toughness than commercially pure tungsten.
The multielement composition of WTaTiVZr accelerates irradiation-induced defect recovery through dynamic annealing.
Reduced residual defect density enables more uniform dislocation motion and plastic deformation.
More efficient defect recovery mitigates irradiation-induced embrittlement.
Ion irradiation at approximately 1000 °C can represent the relevant high-temperature plasma-facing service regime for this comparison.
The relevant irradiation-induced structures include dislocation loops and point-defect clusters.
Recovery of irradiation-induced structures in WTaTiVZr is mediated by dislocation climb and dynamic annealing.
The complex multielement matrix of WTaTiVZr creates local variations in bonding and lattice strain.
Local bonding and lattice-strain variations enhance defect mobility at elevated temperature.
WTaTiVZr undergoes more efficient defect climb and annihilation than pure tungsten.
Irradiation-induced defect accumulation in pure tungsten contributes to embrittlement and inferior plastic deformation.
After identical irradiation and annealing, WTaTiVZr will retain a lower defect density than pure tungsten.
After identical irradiation and annealing, WTaTiVZr will have a more homogeneous dislocation distribution than pure tungsten.
After identical irradiation and annealing, WTaTiVZr will have greater plastic strain than pure tungsten.
After identical irradiation and annealing, WTaTiVZr will have greater fracture toughness than pure tungsten.
The proposed mechanism is applicable near 1000 °C at irradiation fluxes representative of reactor environments but may not apply at substantially lower temperatures or without irradiation.
